content:
The ExaktAI Workspace now also provides a full-featured computer algebra system (CAS)-style interface for Lean. The beta is open to everybody, and we invite you to try it.

The Workspace is a mathematical document environment in which ordinary text, typeset mathematics, executable proof steps, equation labels and explanatory discussion all live together in the same document. As in a CAS workflow, Lean statements are entered in computational regions and executed by Lean, with proofs checked step by step and the goals left after each step shown in sequence inside the document itself. A palette of Lean-aware mathematical symbols is available for input, and steps can be edited and rechecked in place. Mathematical notation is used throughout the document.

The Workspace can also open .lean files natively, and .eai documents can be exported to .lean.

CAS computation is part of the same document model. By default the Workspace uses SymPy and the Python stack for mathematics, and it can drive Maple or Mathematica when they are installed. CAS computations can be inserted between Lean proof steps. A class of CAS results can also be turned into Lean theorem candidates that Lean independently checks.

An AI assistant is also part of the Workspace; it can use your paid AI subscriptions or limited no-charge access to Gemini and Groq without requiring a paid subscription.

For users new to Lean, the Workspace includes a Lean 101 tutorial.

Lean 101 consists of thirteen sections that move from familiar paper proofs to checked Lean proofs. The progression is: state the claim → read the goals → construct the proof → check it. The tutorial uses genuine mathematical examples, with live exercises and editable solutions, and concludes by moving from CAS exploration to independent Lean verification. I would be especially interested in opinions from teachers and mathematically trained newcomers on whether this progression works, as well as feedback from Lean users about the document model and the interaction between formal proof and computational mathematics.

Edgardo Cheb-Terrab
ExaktAI, Canada
